content: Myelosuppression, which includes conditions such as anemia, leukopenia, pancytopenia, and thrombocytopenia, has been observed in patients receiving linezolid. In cases where the outcome is known, hematologic parameters have shown improvement toward baseline levels after discontinuation of linezolid. Weekly monitoring of complete blood counts is recommended for patients on linezolid, especially those undergoing treatment for more than two weeks, those with pre-existing myelosuppression, those taking other medications that suppress bone marrow, or those with chronic infections who have received prior or concurrent antibiotic therapy. If myelosuppression develops or worsens, discontinuation of linezolid should be considered. Peripheral and optic neuropathies have been reported in patients treated with linezolid, particularly in those receiving the drug for durations exceeding the recommended maximum of 28 days. Cases of optic neuropathy leading to vision loss have occurred in patients treated for extended periods beyond this duration. Visual blurring has also been reported in some patients treated for less than 28 days. These neuropathies have been observed in children as well. If patients experience symptoms such as changes in visual acuity, color vision, blurred vision, or visual field defects, an immediate ophthalmic evaluation is advised. Visual function should be monitored in all patients on prolonged linezolid therapy (≥3 months) and in any patient reporting new visual symptoms, regardless of treatment duration. If peripheral or optic neuropathy occurs, the risks and benefits of continuing linezolid therapy should be carefully assessed. Serotonin syndrome, including fatal cases, has been reported when linezolid is co-administered with serotonergic agents such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Linezolid should not be used in patients with carcinoid syndrome or those taking serotonergic medications (e.g., SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, serotonin 5-HT1 receptor agonists, meperidine, bupropion, or buspirone) unless clinically necessary and under close observation for signs of serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like (NMS-like) reactions. In urgent situations where linezolid is required and no alternatives are available, serotonergic medications should be discontinued promptly, and the patient should be monitored for serotonin syndrome symptoms, which include hyperthermia, rigidity, myoclonus, autonomic instability, and mental status changes such as agitation, delirium, or coma. Monitoring for withdrawal symptoms from the serotonergic agent is also necessary. An imbalance in mortality was observed in a clinical study comparing linezolid to vancomycin/dicloxacillin/oxacillin in seriously ill patients with catheter-related bloodstream infections. This imbalance was primarily noted in linezolid-treated patients with Gram-negative pathogens, mixed Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens, or no identified pathogens at baseline. However, this was not observed in patients with Gram-positive infections only. Linezolid is not approved for the treatment of catheter-related bloodstream infections or catheter-site infections and should not be used in such cases. It has no activity against Gram-negative pathogens, and appropriate Gram-negative therapy should be initiated immediately if such pathogens are suspected or confirmed. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including linezolid. CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibiotic use disrupts the normal gut flora, allowing overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in any patient presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after treatment. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of non-C. difficile-targeted antibiotics may be necessary, along with appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy, and surgical evaluation as clinically indicated. Linezolid should not be administered to patients with uncontrolled hypertension, pheochromocytoma, or thyrotoxicosis, or to those taking medications such as sympathomimetic agents (e.g., pseudoephedrine), vasopressors (e.g., epinephrine, norepinephrine), or dopaminergic agents (e.g. Lactic acidosis has been reported in patients receiving linezolid. Symptoms include recurrent nausea, vomiting, unexplained acidosis, or low bicarbonate levels. Patients presenting with these symptoms should undergo immediate medical evaluation. Convulsions have been reported in patients treated with linezolid, including some with a history of seizures or predisposing risk factors for seizures. Symptomatic hypoglycemia has been reported in diabetic patients receiving insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents while on linezolid, a reversible, nonselective monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor. Although a direct causal relationship has not been established, diabetic patients should be warned about the potential for hypoglycemia. If hypoglycemia occurs, adjustments to insulin or oral hypoglycemic agent dosages, or discontinuation of these agents or linezolid, may be necessary. The use of linezolid in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is not recommended, as it is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria.
